opus-5.5.text:
I think, looking back, what he cared about wasn't really whether the project was polished or whether the results were impressive. Honestly, the results were pretty rough. The idea was to take ordinary video and turn it into animation, extracting the motion and the structure from real footage and re-rendering it in a stylized way. At the time I didn't have much background. I was learning computer vision and graphics as I went, hitting walls constantly, and patching things together.

What I think he was watching was how I dealt with those walls. When something didn't work, did I just try random tweaks until it looked okay, or did I go back and ask *why* it failed? Was it the tracking, the segmentation, an assumption about the scene that just doesn't hold for real video? I think he wanted to see whether I could take a fuzzy, messy goal and break it down into problems that could actually be solved, and whether I'd keep going when there was no clear answer in a textbook.

The other thing, I think, was taste, a sense of what's worth doing. Video-to-animation sits right between understanding the real world and generating something new. Even back then I was drawn to that question: how do you get from raw perception of the physical world to something structured that you can manipulate? I think he saw that I wasn't just doing an assignment. I actually *wanted* to know the answer. For a research advisor, that intrinsic drive probably matters more than any specific skill, because skills you can teach, but curiosity and persistence are much harder to install from the outside.

So my understanding is that he was looking for someone who could own a problem, not someone who could follow instructions perfectly. That shaped how I later thought about recruiting students myself. I look less at the résumé and more at whether the person has wrestled with something hard on their own and come out with real understanding, even if the result itself was imperfect.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, I think what he was evaluating wasn't the project itself, it was how I thought about the project.

The video-to-animation idea was honestly pretty naive. I wanted to take a video of a person moving and turn it into a 3D character animation, and at the time I had no real sense of how hard that was. I had read a few papers, I had a rough pipeline in my head, and I was very excited about it.

When I presented it to him, he didn't say "this is good" or "this is bad." He kept asking questions. Why do you want to do this? What happens when the person is occluded? What if the camera moves? If this works, who does it help, and what would they do differently? And I remember feeling a bit frustrated, because I wanted feedback on the method, and he kept pulling me back to the problem.

Later I understood what he was doing. He was checking three things. First, whether I actually cared about the problem or just about the technique. A lot of students fall in love with a tool and go looking for a nail. Second, whether I could tolerate not knowing. Research is mostly being stuck, and he wanted to see how I reacted when he poked a hole in my plan. Did I get defensive, or did I get curious? Third, whether I had taste. Could I tell the difference between a hard problem that mattered and a hard problem that was just hard?

I don't think I passed all three that day. But I think he saw that when he asked a question I couldn't answer, I wrote it down instead of arguing. And I came back a week later with experiments that tried to answer it, even though half of them failed. I think that mattered more to him than the demo.

So if I summarize it, he wasn't looking for someone who already had the right answers. He was looking for someone who would keep asking the right questions after he left the room.
